questions.title: Why enforce non-negative weights in Eq. (1) and omit a bias term?
questions.question_body:
In Section 3.2, the class logit is defined as $\text{logit}_k^i = \max(\mathbf{w}_k, 0) \cdot \mathbf{z}_k^i$, followed by a softmax. This enforces non-negative contributions from rule features and there is no bias term. I am confused about two things:
- If a rule is wrong or should be negative evidence for class $k$, the non-negativity constraint prevents the model from assigning it a negative weight. Doesn't this limit expressivity (e.g., capturing that failing a rule is evidence against a class)?
- Without a bias, when all rules are unsatisfied ($\mathbf{z}_k^i=\mathbf{0}$ for all $k$), all logits are 0 and the softmax becomes uniform. Why is it preferable not to learn class priors via a bias or an "always-on" feature?
Is there an ablation comparing signed weights and/or adding a bias term?

questions.title: How exactly does bagging reduce prompt length, and what are the selection ratios?
questions.question_body:
The paper states that bagging over features and instances mitigates prompt size constraints for rule generation. Could you clarify the concrete procedure?
- Do you sample a subset of columns and a subset of training examples per trial before constructing the prompt? With or without replacement?
- What are the actual sampling ratios for features and instances per dataset (especially for very wide tables like Communities or Myocardial)?
- How do you ensure critical features are not consistently dropped across trials, and do you track coverage of columns across the ensemble?

questions.title: What prevents Step-1 prior-knowledge reasoning from leaking information from examples?
questions.question_body: The prompt design splits reasoning into Step-1 (infer tendencies from prior knowledge only) and Step-2 (use examples plus Step-1 to derive rules). Practically, how do you ensure the LLM does not implicitly use the serialized examples during Step-1? Is Step-1 literally placed before any examples in the prompt, or do you rely solely on instructions? Do you validate that Step-1 content changes meaningfully when examples are removed?

questions.title: How are thresholds for continuous features chosen in generated rules?
questions.question_body: Many tabular rules hinge on thresholds (e.g., "age > 65"). When the LLM proposes such cutoffs, are they expected to come from its prior knowledge, or does it derive them from the few-shot examples (e.g., quantiles)? If the scales/units vary across datasets (like lab values), how do you prevent nonsensical thresholds? Is there any post-hoc calibration or snapping of thresholds to observed percentiles?

questions.title: How is code generated from natural-language rules validated before exec()?
questions.question_body:
Section 3.2 describes prompting the LLM to emit Python code to parse rules and then running it with Python's exec(). This raises concerns:
- Security: Is the code sandboxed (e.g., restricted builtins) to avoid arbitrary execution?
- Correctness: How do you detect silent logical errors (off-by-one thresholds, category name mismatches, handling of missing values) before using the resulting binary features?
- Determinism: Is the code-generation temperature set to a deterministic setting? If not, could parsing failures cause variance across runs?

questions.title: How do you handle missing values or unseen categories when applying rules?
questions.question_body: When generated rules reference features that are missing or categories that were not seen in the few-shot demonstrations, what is the expected behavior of the parser code and the resulting binary feature? Do you default to the rule evaluating to false, skip the rule, or impute? Is there any explicit instruction in the parsing prompt to define this behavior?

questions.title: How are contradictory or overlapping rules across classes handled?
questions.question_body: Because rules are generated independently per class, a sample could satisfy many rules of multiple classes simultaneously. Beyond softmax competition, do you enforce any mutual exclusivity or perform any deduplication/merging of near-duplicate rules across classes? If the same logical rule appears for multiple classes, does that create calibration issues when the number of rules per class is equalized by design?

questions.title: Why is temperature 0.5 considered "sufficiently high" for self-consistency?
questions.question_body: For ensemble diversity you cite self-consistency and set the LLM temperature to 0.5. Self-consistency papers often use relatively high sampling variance and large sample counts. Did you empirically verify that $T=20$ trials and temperature 0.5 yield sufficiently diverse rule sets (e.g., Jaccard distance across rule predicates)? Are there metrics in the appendix quantifying diversity vs. performance?

questions.title: How is the reported "only 30 API queries" computed given T=20 ensembles?
questions.question_body: Implementation details mention $T=20$ ensembles and rule parsing via the LLM, but the runtime section says FeatLLM requires only 30 API queries. Can you break down the exact number of calls per trial for rule generation and for code parsing, and explain how it aggregates to 30 overall? Are multiple rules or classes batched into a single call?

questions.title: Does enforcing non-negativity hinder learning from negative evidence in few-shot settings?
questions.question_body: The rationale for non-negative weights is that LLM-generated features should not reduce a class's likelihood. But in few-shot regimes, false-positive rules may be common. Would allowing negative weights help the model suppress noisy rules more aggressively than relying on weights approaching zero? Did you test a variant with signed weights and $L_1$ regularization to prune bad rules?

questions.title: Is training for 200 epochs on very few shots prone to overfitting?
questions.question_body: You train the linear model for 200 epochs with Adam and choose the epoch via $k$-fold cross-validation on the few shots. With $k$ as small as 2, the validation split is tiny and high-variance. Did you consider early stopping with a patience heuristic, or using explicit regularization (e.g., $L_2$ or $L_1$) to stabilize learning? Any sensitivity analysis on epochs vs. AUROC with $k\in\{2,4\}$?

questions.title: How fair are the baseline comparisons given different LLM backbones and resources?
questions.question_body: TabLLM is run with T0 (not GPT-3.5) due to checkpoint availability, and it uses 4 A100s for model parallelism, while FeatLLM uses GPT-3.5 via API. Could differences in backbone strength and hardware budgets bias the comparisons? Did you include any control where TabLLM or TABLET use the same LLM inference quality (to the extent possible)?

questions.title: How robust is FeatLLM to label imbalance and classes needing different numbers of rules?
questions.question_body: The method fixes the number of rules per class (e.g., $R=10$). If classes differ in complexity or support, a uniform $R$ might be suboptimal. Do you observe any degradation when some classes need far fewer (or more) rules? Did you try adaptive rule counts per class or pruning redundant rules post-generation while keeping the prompt size manageable?

questions.title: What exactly is the selection policy for feature/instance bagging across trials?
questions.question_body:
Bagging is central both for diversity and to fit within prompt limits. Could you specify:
- How many features and examples are sampled per trial as a function of dataset size and column count?
- Whether sampling probabilities are uniform or weighted by any heuristic (e.g., Step-1 importance)?
- If you ever exclude feature descriptions to save tokens, and how you decide when to do so?

questions.title: How do you validate that Step-1 reasoning actually reduces spurious correlations?
questions.question_body: You claim Step-1 (prior knowledge only) helps avoid spurious correlations. Beyond the synthetic spurious-column experiment, did you analyze the textual content of Step-1 vs. final rules to show that Step-1 emphasizes causal features? For example, are there metrics showing increased overlap between Step-1 highlighted features and the final rule predicates, or reduced use of irrelevant features compared to a baseline without Step-1?

questions.title: How do you control for leakage when using recent datasets to avoid pretraining overlap?
questions.question_body: For Cultivars and NHANES, you argue they post-date GPT-3.5-0613 pretraining. However, exact pretraining cutoffs and data sources are opaque. Did you also test with synthetic feature descriptions (to avoid web-retrieved wording), or ablate feature descriptions entirely to ensure performance is not driven by memorized text? Any reproducible checks for leakage you can share?

questions.title: How are categorical variables with many levels represented and matched in rules?
questions.question_body: For high-cardinality categoricals, rules like "occupation is X" can be too specific or brittle. Do you instruct the LLM to cluster categories (e.g., via semantic similarity) or to prefer broader conditions (e.g., "occupation in {X, Y, Z}")? When the parser turns text into code, how do you handle category name normalization (case, punctuation) and unseen levels at test time?

questions.title: Why average probabilities across ensembles instead of stacking or logit averaging?
questions.question_body: At inference you average per-trial class probabilities. Did you try averaging logits (before softmax), or learning a lightweight stacking model on top of the per-trial probabilities? In few-shot regimes stacking risks overfitting, but a simple logit average might improve calibration. Any comparisons in the appendix?

questions.title: How general is FeatLLM beyond classification to regression or ranking tasks?
questions.question_body: The current formulation produces binary rule-based features and uses a softmax over classes. For regression, would you just replace softmax and cross-entropy with a linear combination and a regression loss? Would you still enforce non-negativity of weights? Are there any results or caveats when rules need to express continuous relationships rather than discrete class conditions?

questions.title: How do you ensure rule expressivity is sufficient for complex interactions?
questions.question_body: The response instruction allows logical operators like AND/OR inside a rule, but each rule is ultimately a single binary feature. Can the LLM propose arithmetic combinations (e.g., $\text{BMI} = \text{weight}/\text{height}^2$) or temporal patterns, or is it limited to threshold and set-membership predicates? If richer expressions are allowed, how is parsing specified and validated?
